definition: Sardonic means grimly mocking and scornful — humor with dark disdain running underneath it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sardonic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sardonic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The tow-truck driver kept a sardonic sign bolted above the winch — 'Your shortcut, my salary' — and waved pleasantly at every car in the ditch.
Wry is milder than sardonic — a small, crooked smile at life's ironies, affectionate as often as not, with none of sardonic's scorn.
Sneering goes further than sardonic: the humor drains away entirely and open contempt is all that's left on the face.

Mocking is the broad word for making fun of something, from playground teasing to open ridicule — the mockery can even be affectionate. Sardonic is mockery served cold: the laugh has scorn in it, and the speaker sounds half-finished with the world he's laughing at.

Cynical describes a belief — that people act from self-interest and every promise is for sale. Sardonic is what that belief sounds like when it smiles: the dry, dark joke a cynic makes instead of an argument.
sincere and serious, meaning every word straight
amused in a warm way, with no scorn in the laugh

The trail behind sardonic dead-ends in legend: Greek sardonios was tied — by story, not by sound law — to Sardinia and its face-twisting plant, and the root built nothing else in English. There is no everyday cousin to reuse; the word stands alone, smirking.
Sardonic means grimly mocking and scornful — humor with dark disdain running underneath it.
After the third round of budget cuts, the lab director's memos turned sardonic: 'Good news — headquarters believes we can cure the disease with two beakers and the interns' optimism.'

Sardonic is more precise than 'sarcastic' because sarcasm is a technique — saying the opposite of what you mean — while sardonic names the temperature: cold, scornful amusement, usually aimed at fate, folly, or the whole absurd situation.
A sardonic speaker isn't erupting in anger; the joke is how little he expects anymore.
Sardonic is the reviewer's word for humor that scorns what it describes — a sardonic narrator, a sardonic aside.
Two unit-mates patrol the same block: acerbic stings with a sour, witty bite, and vitriolic has stopped joking altogether.
Sardonic is the coolest of the three — it mocks darkly and keeps its seat.

Nobody reads Ferro's restaurant column for the recipes.

They read it for sentences like his verdict on the city's most expensive tasting menu: 'Nine courses, each one an apology for the last.' The style is sardonic — every joke lands with a curl of scorn in it, as if the whole industry had personally let him down.
Young chefs claim not to read him, though their sous-chefs quietly report otherwise.
Admirers point out the jokes are genuinely funny; Ferro's targets notice only that the laughter is never warm.
